proposals.relationship: Ryan uses Joan Wallach Scott and Louise Tilly’s joint account of enduring links between households, factories and labor to challenge a simple identification of industrialization with the isolated nuclear family.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Cradle2 credits Joan Scott and Louise Tilly jointly and uses their findings in its methodological argument. Louise Tilly has no endpoint and is not Charles Tilly; available Joan Wallach Scott identity is independently corroborated by her official Cambridge Tilly–Scott collaboration abstract/metadata(2014issue/2015online), not an additional body-reading claim. Specific published original and Ryan endnote unread; resource use does not imply personal training or agreement with all their writings.
primary_locators: Cradle introduction2,paragraph beginning Until very recently

proposals.relationship: Ryan uses Ariès’s historical account of childhood as an example of family change that cannot be measured only by household size or structure.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Cradle2–3 moves from criticism of the industrialization/nuclear-family equation to a named array of historical changes;3calls Ariès’s account classic. This is a bounded methodological resource, not endorsement of all childhood chronology or assertion of first personal reading. Original Ariès work and endnote not checked.

proposals.relationship: Ryan uses Stone’s tripartite account of family change between1500and1800 as a resource for examining changing relationships and sentiments beyond household structure.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Cradle3 expressly names Stone’s typology alongside Ariès,Shorter and Levine; later paragraph contrasts nineteenth-century American inquiry with directions opened by Stone/Levine. Positive particular resource does not establish wholesale adoption of Stone’s scheme, every date or a personal relationship. Original work and Ryan endnote unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan uses Katz’s study of Hamilton as a comparative resource for locating Utica’s families within the economic and social organization of nineteenth-century cities.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Cradle3names Katz’s Hamilton monograph among quantitative urban family studies;5explicitly uses Hamilton’s mixed factories,crafts,commerce,mobility and immigration to contextualize Utica. Her3–4reservation about narrow statistical pictures remains a general methodological qualification, not automatically a work-specific denunciation of Katz. Prefacexivalso credits Katz among collective manuscript readers, corroborating engagement without inventing particular advice. Original Katz book and endnotes unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan draws inspiration from Arendt’s account of a public realm of speech and action while redirecting it toward the historically varied social spaces of American cities.
proposals.evidence_note: Own CivicWars5–6 explicitly records intellectual indebtedness to Arendt’s lofty formulation;8returns to the public as a sphere of discourse and action.5also retains Hanna Pitkin’s criticism of elitist assumptions and exclusion, not unqualified allegiance to Arendt’s model. Pitkin endpoint absent; original Arendt/Pitkin texts and missing book endnotes unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan explicitly identifies Habermas’s account of the public sphere as an indispensable guide to her research into public life beyond the state.
proposals.evidence_note: Own CivicWars6 says the work guided research for this book and locates public activity in newspapers,cafes and clubs. The same discussion qualifies its bourgeois eighteenth-century limits and turns to Dewey/Lefort for broader possibilities. This specific positive use coexists with existing1468Ryan→Habermas critique explicitly mediated by Fraser; neither relation is reduced to an all-purpose agreement/rejection. Habermas original and Ryan missing endnotes unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan uses Tocqueville’s attention to association,urban sociability and the press to guide her historical inquiry into American public life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own CivicWars8–9 explicitly treats Tocqueville as a guide to the story and14uses his account of newspaper communication.10–11also tests the limits of homogeneous village images against her heterogeneous cities;8includes Lefort’s quoted Tocqueville interpretation. Resource use is therefore qualified and includes observed conceptual mediation, not an assertion about personal first reading or endorsement of every democratic claim. Tocqueville original and Ryan missing endnotes unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan contrasts Turner’s frontier-centered account of American individual freedom with Tocqueville’s emphasis on dense association,using the latter to frame her study of city publics.
proposals.evidence_note: Own CivicWars9 explicitly juxtaposes supposedly open western spaces with people gathering in towns. This is a named interpretive comparison within Ryan’s urban framing, not a wholesale refutation of Turner’s thesis or proof she adopted a Turner school. Original Turner text and Ryan endnote unread.

proposals.relationship: Ryan develops a spatial history of public life through city streets,squares,ceremonies,associations and government decisions in nineteenth-century New York,New Orleans and San Francisco.
proposals.evidence_note: Own CivicWars2–3,14–18 explains a spatial strategy and three-city comparison for recovering varied participation and exclusion. Policy/cityhalls16–17remain part of this inquiry, rather than reducing the project to rhetoric alone. Bounded methodological contribution in this work, not founding the whole field or claiming every urban resident could participate equally. Selected introduction only; empirical chapters and absent notes unread.
